stories.title: New York Office Market Leaders On Talent Retention, Affordability and AI
stories.excerpt: The movers and shakers of New York City’s office market converged upon Rudin’s 3 Times Square on Wednesday for Commercial Observer’s 2026 State of Office forum. Despite the competitive nature of their business, the gathered landlords, brokers and executives seemed almost convivial. The warm atmosphere was understandable, fostered by a scorching hot 2026 office market. The gathering, kick-started by Hannah Rosenberg, senior analyst of portfolio management at U.S. Logistics Partners, was a victory lap for 2026 successes — record rents, a booming technology industry, months of leasing momentum and new supply lows — yet sour notes of rising interest rates and declining affordability tempered celebrations. The balance between the boom time and challenges ahead was perhaps best described by Bruce Mosler, chairman of Cushman & Wakefield’s global brokerage and moderator of the forum’s first panel. “We’re in a place that we haven’t been for a long time, a very healthy place in New York, and now the spillover from everything that’s happening in Class A is affecting the lease-up in Class B, and even parts of downtown,” Mosler said. “With that said, we also have rising interest rates, and we have inflation on the horizon.” Mosler’s introductory conversation with Bill Rudin, co-executive chairman of Rudin, and Edward Forst, administrator of the U.S. General Services Administration, covered familiar ground for office market observers. The best offices are filling up, the industry veterans agreed, and New York City remains a magnet for talent. Just look at 350 Park Avenue, Rudin’s 1.9 million-square-foot trophy tower with hedge fund Citadel, or at Rudin’s 32 Avenue of the Americas property. “Frankly, the space was sitting for a significant time,” Rudin said. “In the last six months, we have signed a lease for 100,000 feet, and we have a 200,000-foot lease out.” Bill Rudin (right) speaks on a panel with Edward Forst (left) and Bruce Mosler at the Commercial Ob
bullets: NYC office market posting record rents, booming tech demand, new supply at decade lows in 2026.
Rising interest rates and declining affordability creating headwinds despite strong leasing momentum.
Landlords and brokers convened at 3 Times Square forum celebrating 'very healthy' market conditions.
stories.summary: New York City's office market is experiencing a strong recovery with record rents, robust technology sector leasing, and months of positive momentum, but rising interest rates and declining affordability are tempering enthusiasm. New supply has fallen to historic lows, with record leasing activity through 2026. Despite the boom, market participants acknowledge structural challenges ahead.
stories.impact: Tight office supply and strong Class A demand in Manhattan signals sustained pricing power for premium product, but rising rates and affordability pressures may soon suppress corporate demand. This creates a narrowing window for multifamily developers to acquire land and underwrite new supply in Manhattan and Brooklyn submarkets before capitalization rates compress further or financing conditions tighten—especially for workforce housing near employment centers.

stories.title: Fortress Buys Assisted Living Center in Delray Beach, Fla.
stories.excerpt: Fortress Investment Group paid at least $25.8 million for an assisted living facility in Delray Beach, Fla. The 126,918-square-foot property sits adjacent to South Military Trail at 4840 West Atlantic Avenue, about two miles west of Interstate 95. The 4.2-acre asset, constructed in 2018, houses 118 beds. The transaction comes out to about $218,220 per bed, though the total sale price is likely higher to include for the facility’s furniture and business operation. New York-based Fortress Investment Group assumed the seller’s loan from Atlantic Union Bank with $22.2 million in outstanding debt and increased it by $3 million. The $25.3 million financing is scheduled to mature in 2030. The seller, an entity tied to Capital Health Group‘s Kenneth Assiran, purchased the development parcel for just under $4 million in 2015. There’s been an uptick in the sales of nursing homes and assisted living facilities across South Florida as the state’s senior population is expected to grow by 2.2 million by 2040, according to state estimates. Recent transactions include Welltower’s $49 million acquisition of a 120-unit in Broward County this week and Artemis Real Estate Partners’ $140 million purchase of a 7.2-acre asset in August. Assiran could not be reached for comment, while a spokesperson for Fortress Investment Group did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Julia Echikson can be reached at jechikson@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Fortress Investment Group paid $25.8M for 118-bed assisted living facility in Delray Beach, Florida.
Florida's senior population projected to grow 2.2M by 2040, driving uptick in senior housing sales.
Asset purchased for $4M in 2015; transaction reflects 545% value appreciation over 11 years.
stories.summary: Fortress Investment Group acquired a 118-bed assisted living center in Delray Beach for $25.8 million, assuming $22.2 million in Atlantic Union Bank debt and adding $3 million new financing. The transaction implies $218,000+ per bed and reflects accelerating sales activity in senior housing across South Florida, driven by projected 2.2 million growth in the state's senior population by 2040.
stories.impact: Senior housing cap rates and debt availability remain favorable even as Fortress recycles capital into assisted living. For multifamily developers, this signals that age-restricted and 55+ communities near South Florida retirement destinations (Delray, Naples, The Villages submarkets) will see sustained demand and may outperform traditional rental apartment delivery; consider land acquisition in these corridors or mixed-use senior-inclusive projects to capture demographic tailwinds.

stories.title: Pura Vida Miami Makes New England Debut with Harvard Square Café
stories.excerpt: Pura Vida Miami has opened a new location in Cambridge’s Harvard Square, marking the popular café brand’s first foray into the Northeast U.S. The national chain of wellness-oriented cafés has opened its doors at 95 Mount Auburn St., occupying the entire ground floor of the three-story, Class A office and retail building neighboring Harvard University. Boston-based The Bulfinch Companies, which owns the 12,984-square-foot property through an affiliate, signed the purveyor of cold-pressed juices and açaí bowls as a tenant in the first quarter. Bulfinch appointed Boston Realty Advisors as the building’s retail leasing agent last year. Founded in Miami in 2012, and currently headquartered in the city’s Wynwood district, Pura Vida Miami has grown to more than 50 locations across seven states and Washington, D.C., with the latest addition marking its first café in Massachusetts. “Harvard Square is experiencing a genuine retail resurgence, and Pura Vida Miami’s arrival is a strong example of the caliber of brands choosing to invest here,” said Michael Wilcox, Managing Director of Leasing at Bulfinch in a statement. Image courtesy of The Bulfinch Companies. The post Pura Vida Miami Makes New England Debut with Harvard Square Café appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Pura Vida Miami opens flagship café at Harvard Square, 95 Mount Auburn St., Cambridge, Massachusetts.
Wellness café chain expanded to 50+ locations across 7 states; first Northeast entry signals brand scaling.
Class A office/retail building leased at 100% occupancy; Harvard Square retail resurgence underway.
stories.summary: Pura Vida Miami, a Miami-based wellness café chain with 50+ locations, opened its first Northeast location at 12,984-square-foot Class A office and retail property in Harvard Square, Cambridge. The Bulfinch Companies owns the three-story building through an affiliate. The tenant success reflects a broader retail resurgence in Harvard Square and signals strong demand for upscale, health-conscious food and beverage tenants.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact on multifamily development. However, the retail leasing activity and brand expansion into Boston signals education/research hub vitality and discretionary spending power among Harvard-adjacent white-collar workforce—a positive underlying demand signal for multifamily in Cambridge, Somerville, and nearby transit-accessible neighborhoods near universities and biotech clusters.

stories.title: Alloy Completes Lease-Up of Spec Lab Space at Sorrento Mesa Project
stories.excerpt: Alloy Properties has signed Biora Therapeutics to a 19,560-square-foot lease at Elements by Alloy Properties, a 290,000-square-foot life science campus located at 10201–10241 Wateridge Cir. in San Diego’s Sorrento Mesa submarket. The transaction marks the third lease completed at Elements in the past six months and completes the lease-up of the project’s available spec lab space. “While the broader life science market continues to face challenges, Elements has demonstrated that tenants remain willing to commit to exceptional laboratory environments that offer quality, flexibility and immediate occupancy,” said Alicia Hinds, COO of Alloy Properties. “The successful lease-up of our original three floors of spec suites reinforces our confidence in the project and supports our decision to move forward with the next phase of development.” JLL’s Tony Russell and Tim Olson represented Alloy Properties in the Biora Therapeutics lease. Biora Therapeutics was represented by Greg Bisconti and Justin Venckus, also of JLL. The post Alloy Completes Lease-Up of Spec Lab Space at Sorrento Mesa Project appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Alloy Properties leases 19,560 SF to Biora Therapeutics at Elements life science campus, San Diego.
Third lease in 6 months completes lease-up of 290,000 SF project's spec lab space at Sorrento Mesa.
Life science market facing headwinds, but quality, flexibility, immediate occupancy drive tenant commitment.
stories.summary: Alloy Properties signed Biora Therapeutics to a 19,560-square-foot lab lease at Elements by Alloy Properties, a 290,000-square-foot life science campus in San Diego's Sorrento Mesa submarket. The transaction marks the third lease in six months and completes lease-up of available spec lab space. Despite industry-wide challenges, high-quality lab environments with flexibility and immediate occupancy are attracting tenants.
stories.impact: Life science real estate remains differentiated and resilient in San Diego despite sector-wide headwinds, signaling sustained tenant demand for built-to-suit and flex lab space. For multifamily developers, this underscores that proximity to biotech/pharma clusters (Sorrento Mesa, La Jolla, UTC) supports workforce multifamily demand; consider land assembly near life science employment centers and mixed-use projects with ground-floor lab or flex space to capture both scientific workforce and spillover office/medical demand.

stories.title: Office Vacancy Eases in Q3 as New Supply Nears Record Lows
stories.excerpt: The U.S. office market continued its recovery in Q3, according to national reports from CBRE, JLL, Cushman & Wakefield, Colliers and Lee & Associates. All reported lower vacancy year over year, new construction fell to its lowest level in decades, and demand continued to favor higher-quality buildings. Vacancy Declines Everywhere Colliers reported a 17.7% vacancy, representing a 60 basis-point decrease from the year before, and the lowest since Q4 2023. CBRE also noted a 60 bps drop, with vacancy at 18.2%; a fifth consecutive quarterly decline. Cushman & Wakefield had vacancy at 19.8%, down 30 bps from its Q3 2025 peak. JLL reported a vacancy of 21.5%, while Lee & Associates ended up at 13.8%, about 20 bps below its 2025 high. Leasing Favors the Best CBRE said leasing rose 4% year-over-year to 63.8 million square feet, the highest quarterly total since the fourth quarter of 2024, and expects 2026 leasing to surpass its 2022 record. JLL said leases signed over the past 12 months carried an average footprint increase of 13%, even as companies continue to downsize. All agreed that quality continued to drive demand. Cushman & Wakefield said Class A buildings accounted for two-thirds of third-quarter leasing, well above the 10-year average of 61%. Colliers pointed to demand from AI and tech occupiers. At the same time, Lee & Associates credited stricter attendance requirements at major financial firms and AI-driven startups in San Francisco and Silicon Valley, CA. Construction Pipeline Hits Bottom CBRE said completions fell 76% year-over-year to 1.5 million square feet, putting 2026 on track for the lowest annual total since the company started tracking in 1990. JLL said 9.6 million square feet were removed from inventory for conversions or redevelopment during the quarter; completions totaled 3.5 million square feet, and inventory has fallen by more than 45 million square feet since late 2023. bullets: U.S. office vacancy eased in Q3; new construction fell to lowest level in decades—76% YoY decline.
CBRE projects 2026 leasing will surpass 2022 record; Class A buildings captured 2/3 of Q3 leasing.
AI/tech occupiers and stricter attendance mandates at financial firms driving demand in San Francisco, Silicon Valley.
stories.summary: The U.S. office market continued recovery in Q3 with lower vacancy year-over-year and new construction at historic lows (76% YoY decline in completions). CBRE expects 2026 leasing to surpass 2022 record at 63.8 million SF in Q3 alone. Class A buildings accounted for two-thirds of Q3 leasing, well above the 10-year average. AI-driven startups and financial firms' stricter attendance policies are concentrating demand in San Francisco and Silicon Valley.
stories.impact: Tight office supply and rising Class A selectivity means corporate tenant flight to premium, modern buildings will persist through 2026, reinforcing rent growth in CBD submarkets with top-tier office stock. For multifamily developers, this amplifies demand for workforce housing near major financial and tech employment centers (Manhattan, Midtown, San Francisco, Silicon Valley, Boston); early-stage land acquisition and entitlements in these nodes—especially transit-adjacent submarkets—will be critical before rents fully reflect recovered job density and office absorption.

stories.title: ‍Coral Gables, Fla., Spends $24M to Expand City Hall‍
stories.excerpt: After years of off-and-on negotiations, the City of Coral Gables, Fla., now owns the entire 400 block of Biltmore Way. The city paid $24 million to acquire the four-story, 53,029-square-foot Biltmore Medical Center at 475-495 Biltmore Way, according to Blanca Commercial Real Estate, the leasing agent for the property. The medical center was last sold to Jacksonville-based ShareMD in 2019 for $14.6 million, according to county property records. The city began discussing a purchase of the building about that time, the Miami Herald reported. The building’s occupancy rose from 82 percent to 94 percent and net operating income increased by 40 percent during ShareMD’s ownership, Blanca Commercial Real Estate said. The deal comes as a multimillion-dollar renovation of the historic city hall is set to begin nearby. The Biltmore Medical Center is set to provide offices for development staff and administrative departments. The city commission approved the intent to purchase the property earlier this year. The city tapped ShareMD’s property management affiliate, Medicus Asset Management, to oversee the building for a one-year term following the sale. Jeff Ostrowski can be reached at jostrowski@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: City of Coral Gables, Florida purchased Biltmore Medical Center, 475-495 Biltmore Way, for $24 million.
Four-story, 53,029 SF office/medical building acquired to house city development and administrative staff.
Occupancy rose from 82% to 94% under prior ownership (ShareMD); $24M purchase reflects 64% premium over 2019 acquisition price of $14.6M.
stories.summary: Coral Gables acquired the Biltmore Medical Center, a 53,029-square-foot, four-story office and medical building, for $24 million to consolidate city development and administrative departments during a multimillion-dollar city hall renovation. The property was last purchased in 2019 for $14.6 million. Occupancy and NOI improved significantly under prior owner ShareMD, rising to 94% occupancy and 40% NOI growth.
stories.impact: Limited direct multifamily impact. However, city capital deployment into office consolidation and administrative infrastructure signals sustained Coral Gables confidence in long-term growth trajectory and community development investment. This reinforces continued economic vitality in South Florida's affluent coastal submarkets, supporting underlying demand for Class A and lifestyle multifamily product in Coral Gables, Miami Beach, and adjacent high-income neighborhoods; monitor for follow-on municipal or private redevelopment activity on the 400 block of Biltmore Way.

stories.title: MetLife Expands to 500K SF at 200 Park Avenue
stories.excerpt: MetLife isn’t letting anyone forget whose name is on the building. The insurance company signed an expansion deal at the Irvine Company’s 200 Park Avenue — better known as the MetLife Building — to grow its footprint from roughly 450,000 to roughly 500,000 square feet in the 59-story building, according to CBRE. The new 10-year expansion lease was for 47,628 square feet, the brokerage said. MetLife was last known to have leased roughly 400,000 square feet in its namesake building, and it’s not known when it expanded to roughly 450,000 square feet. CBRE did not disclose the asking rent, but the average office asking rent in Midtown was ​​$86.49 per square foot in October, according to CBRE’s monthly office report. CBRE’s Mary Ann Tighe, Howard Fiddle, Peter Turchin, Evan Haskell, Brett Shannon and Julia Passante negotiated the deal on behalf of the landlord, while Patrick Murphy at JLL represented MetLife. MetLife owned the property starting in 1981 when it bought it from Pan American Airways for $400 million. The insurance firm later sold the building to Tishman Speyer and Irvine Company in 2005 for $1.72 billion — a record price, at the time. Its last publicly announced lease extension for its office space on Park Avenue was in 2023, when it committed to another 11 years in place. The deal marked the sixth largest office lease of that year. Other tenants in the building include law firm Gibson Dunn, which renewed its 361,569-square-foot office in January, as well as law firm Winston & Strawn, which also renewed its 237,815-square-foot lease in December 2024. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: MetLife expanded office footprint from ~450,000 SF to 500,000 SF at 200 Park Avenue, Midtown Manhattan.
10-year lease for 47,628 SF at Midtown average asking rent of $86.49/SF as of October 2026.
Anchor tenant commitment reinforces Midtown CBD leasing momentum and Class A building resilience.
stories.summary: MetLife signed a 10-year expansion lease for 47,628 square feet at 200 Park Avenue (the MetLife Building), growing its total footprint from roughly 450,000 to 500,000 square feet. Midtown average office asking rent stood at $86.49 per square foot in October 2026. The deal signals sustained corporate commitment to the CBD and iconic office towers.
stories.impact: Anchor tenant expansion in Midtown—especially by a Fortune 500 insurer—reinforces CBD job density and prestige office demand, supporting continued rent growth and pricing power in Manhattan core submarkets. For multifamily developers, MetLife's long-term commitment to Midtown signals sustained white-collar employment concentration; prioritize acquisition and development of workforce-priced rental housing (1BR/2BR flex units) within 0.5-mile radius of Midtown CBD to capture extended lease-up windows and rent growth as office absorption continues post-recovery.

stories.title: Vivmark Touts Integration and Growth in First Quarterly Earnings Call
stories.excerpt: Oh, it’s good to be the nation’s largest publicly traded apartment owner Vivmark Residential, the real estate investment trust (REIT) formed earlier this year by the thunderclap merger between AvalonBay Communities and Equity Residential, turned in its first quarterly report card on Thursday. The results were as hefty as you might expect for a company with more than 184,000 apartments in high-priced markets such as the San Francisco, Washington, D.C., Boston and New York areas and a $4.4 billion development pipeline. Executives on Thursday’s earnings call credited a better-than-expected integration of Equity Residential and AvalonBay for the results. As a sign of that smoother integration, the REIT said its merger-related costs were running around $725 million, or $25 million below an initial estimate. “Our primary focus right now is on execution — execution of the underlying business and execution of our integration,” Benjamin Schall, Vivmark’s CEO and president (who held identical positions at AvalonBay), said on the call. “The term I use internally is ‘We need to get the core right.’” Schall also said that the company planned to scale relatively fast. “We have defined our vision as Vivmark Residential is going to be the most trusted and best-performing rental housing company in the country,” he said. Vivmark reported $1.19 billion in revenue for the third quarter, and its net operating income was $800.76 million despite a more than $747 million loss for the quarter. Funds from operations (FFO) — a measure of a REIT’s cash flow — was 8 cents a share, and its core FFO was $1.03 a share. The results covered Vivmark’s performance following the mid-August closing of the merger, and AvalonBay’s performance alone in the two-plus weeks before that. (AvalonBay was the accounting acquirer under the deal.) bullets: Vivmark Residential (AvalonBay + Equity Residential merger) reports 184,000+ apartments, $4.4B development pipeline.
Merger-related costs running $725M, $25M below initial budget; integration tracking ahead of schedule.
Largest publicly traded multifamily REIT positioned in high-priced markets: SF, DC, Boston, New York.
stories.summary: Vivmark Residential, formed in 2026 by the merger of AvalonBay Communities and Equity Residential, reported strong integration progress in its first quarterly earnings call. The REIT operates 184,000+ apartments across premium markets (San Francisco, Washington D.C., Boston, New York) and maintains a $4.4 billion development pipeline. Merger-related costs are tracking $25 million below the initial $750 million estimate at $725 million.
stories.impact: Vivmark's scale, capital efficiency, and aggressive development pipeline signal heightened competitive intensity in high-barrier-to-entry coastal markets (SF, DC, Boston, Manhattan) where the merged REIT has unmatched land holdings and entitlements. For other multifamily developers, this consolidation raises the bar on execution speed, cost control, and market timing; smaller regional developers should focus on secondary/tertiary markets or niche product (senior, workforce, mixed-use) where Vivmark's scale offers less advantage. Monitor Vivmark's pipeline density and lease-up velocities as benchmarks for underwriting assumptions in comparable submarkets.
